# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and pharmacology

Heart failure (HF) management has long centred on antagonising maladaptive neurohormonal pathways—particularly the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system—while comparatively neglecting the counter-regulatory natriuretic peptide system [1]. Natriuretic peptides promote natriuresis, vasodilatation, and inhibition of fibrosis, hypertrophy, and RAAS activity, but are degraded by the enzyme neprilysin [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan (formerly LCZ696) is a first-in-class angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). After ingestion, it delivers systemic exposure to AHU377, a neprilysin inhibitor pro-drug, and valsartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker; AHU377 is then rapidly metabolised by non-specific esterases to the active neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657. Earlier dual ACE/neprilysin inhibition with omapatrilat was abandoned because of angioedema risk, prompting the deliberate combination of neprilysin inhibition with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor [1].

## Pivotal trial in HFrEF: PARADIGM-HF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established ARNI as transformative therapy for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). In this double-blind trial, 8442 patients with class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less were randomly assigned to receive either LCZ696 (200 mg twice daily) or enalapril (10 mg twice daily), in addition to recommended therapy. The trial was stopped prematurely after a median follow-up of 27 months on the recommendation of the data safety monitoring board owing to compelling evidence in favour of sacubitril/valsartan. It significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation by 20% compared with enalapril [2]. Benefit was consistent regardless of background therapy and across baseline systolic blood pressure strata [3,4]. Because inhibition of ACE and co-inhibition of ACE and neprilysin may increase the risk of angioedema, the design incorporated sequential run-ins and two wash-out periods to minimise overlapping ACE and neprilysin inhibition [5].

## Mechanisms: reverse remodelling and biomarkers

The mechanistic basis of clinical benefit was clarified by subsequent studies. In PROVE-HF, an open-label study, treatment reduced NT-proBNP concentrations, and the investigators sought to determine whether these changes correlated with measures of cardiac volume and function [6]. Over 12 months, changes in NT-proBNP correlated with progressive improvements in LVEF, LV end-diastolic and end-systolic volume indices, left atrial volume index, and E/e′ ratio [6]. In contrast, the EVALUATE-HF trial demonstrated that the benefits are not explained by effects on central arterial stiffness. EVALUATE-HF randomised 464 participants with HFrEF to sacubitril-valsartan or enalapril for 12 weeks, finding greater reductions in mean arterial pressure and pulse pressure, though no significant effect on aortic impedance [7]. Phase II groundwork in HFpEF came from PARAMOUNT. PARAMOUNT was a phase 2 randomised double-blind trial of LCZ696 in patients with NYHA class II–III HF, LVEF ≥45%, and elevated NT-proBNP [8], demonstrating a greater NT-proBNP reduction versus valsartan.

## Acute and post-discharge initiation

Whereas PARADIGM-HF enrolled stable ambulatory outpatients, later trials examined in-hospital initiation. PIONEER-HF was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial conducted at 129 US sites comparing in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril for 8 weeks among 881 patients admitted for acute decompensated HF with reduced ejection fraction and hemodynamic stability [9]. Sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a greater reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril (-47% vs -25%), with similar rates of adverse reactions [9]. Clinical outcomes favoured ARNI in an exploratory analysis [10], and benefit extended to high-risk subgroups [11] and across achieved dose levels [12]. The open-label TRANSITION study randomised patients stratified by pre-admission RAAS-inhibitor therapy to start sacubitril/valsartan either pre- or post-discharge, supporting feasible early initiation [13].

## Across the ejection fraction spectrum: PARAGON-HF

PARAGON-HF tested ARNI in higher ejection fractions. It enrolled patients with NYHA class II–IV HF, ejection fraction of 45% or higher, elevated natriuretic peptides, and structural heart disease, randomised to sacubitril–valsartan or valsartan [14]. Sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total HF hospitalisations and cardiovascular death among patients with an ejection fraction of 45% or higher [14]. The primary endpoint was narrowly missed (HR 0.87; P = 0.059); subgroup analysis suggested benefit at lower LVEF (below the median) [14]. A pooled HFrEF/HFpEF analysis reinforced an attenuation of effect with rising LVEF. Across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan was superior to RAAS inhibition for first cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation, with treatment effect varying by ejection fraction [15]. Women and patients with prior HF hospitalisation appeared to derive greater benefit [16,17].

## Worsening HF with higher ejection fraction and post-MI

PARAGLIDE-HF extended this work to recent worsening HF events. Mentz et al. reported angiotensin–neprilysin inhibition in patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction and worsening heart failure [18]. In pooled analyses of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan reduced cardiovascular and renal events, particularly among those with LVEF below normal, regardless of care setting [19]. In acute MI, however, ARNI did not outperform an ACE inhibitor. In PARADISE-MI, sacubitril–valsartan was not associated with a significantly lower incidence of death from cardiovascular causes or incident heart failure than ramipril among patients with acute myocardial infarction [20].

## Guidelines and clinical implications

Contemporary guidelines reflect this evidence. The 2021 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure provide recommendations on ARNI use [21], and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline highlights treatment strategies including SGLT2 inhibitors and ARNI [22]. ARNI is recommended as a foundational therapy (replacing ACE inhibitors/ARBs) in chronic HFrEF, and represents high-value care [22]. Open questions remain regarding optimal sequencing relative to SGLT2 inhibitors, dosing in patients who cannot reach target doses, and the role of ARNI in HFpEF and after MI. In summary, ARNI therapy markedly improves outcomes in HFrEF, with effect attenuating as ejection fraction rises, and a benefit driven substantially by reverse cardiac remodelling.
